intents.text: I'm glad you're paying attention to this — it's exactly the kind of thing worth taking seriously. **Heads up:** this is outside the course library I'm grounded in, so treat what I say as a starting point, not a clinical or policy answer. If your roommate is in immediate danger, contact campus safety or 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) right away. Otherwise, the usual path is: reach out to your **RA**, your campus **counseling center**, or a **Dean of Students / care team** referral — they're trained for exactly this. You don't have to diagnose anything; just describe what you've observed and let them take it from there. Want me to point you to the wellness module in your library, or run a quick scenario on hard conversations?
suggested: How do I start the conversation?

intents.text: Quick caveat — campus policy isn't something I have inside my course library, so I can't quote your school's exact rule. **For anything that could affect your standing, check the student handbook or ask your RA / Dean of Students directly.** In general, most campuses treat off-campus conduct under a code-of-conduct clause when it touches school-sponsored events, hazing, or anything that creates risk for other students. The handbook usually spells out where the line is. Want me to point you to the academic-integrity / conduct module in your library so you can practice the framework?

Good instinct to pause and check before reacting. **Heads up:** the specifics of mandatory reporting depend on your company policy, jurisdiction, and role — that's outside what I can answer definitively, so loop in **HR or your supervisor's supervisor** for the binding answer. The general shape is: (1) **document** what was said, when, where, and witnesses, (2) **acknowledge** the report-out from your direct report and thank them for raising it, (3) most workplace harassment policies make leads **mandatory reporters** once a complaint is named — meaning you forward it, you don't sit on it, and (4) avoid investigating yourself. Want me to pull up the workplace-conduct module in your library, or run a {practiceWord} on receiving a sensitive disclosure?

Yes — say something now, and don't worry about looking difficult. **Quick caveat:** I'm giving you general safety guidance, not a site-specific procedure, so confirm the right call with your supervisor or safety officer. The basics: an unlabeled container near an ignition source breaks two rules at once (HazCom labeling + ignition-source control). Right now: **move the container away from the flame** if it's safe to do so, **isolate** the area, and **flag your shift lead or safety officer immediately**. Don't try to identify the contents yourself — without a label or SDS, you can't trust your nose. Want me to pull up the relevant chapter in your safety library, or run a {practiceWord} on speaking up early?
Default isolation for an unknown {scenarioWord} starts at **50 meters** and grows with vapor, fire, or victim symptoms. Treat it as a *living* number — re-check it on every wind shift.
**qSOFA** flags risk, not diagnosis. Two of three (RR ≥ 22, altered mentation, SBP ≤ 100) earns immediate re-evaluation and starts the bundle clock — it doesn't replace clinical judgment.

card.summary: Triage-side recognition tool. Two of three positive criteria → escalate, don't wait on labs.

intents.text: The **hour-1 bundle**: lactate → blood cultures (before antibiotics when feasible) → broad-spectrum antibiotics → 30 mL/kg crystalloid → vasopressors if MAP < 65 after fluids. **Velocity beats perfect ordering**.
Lead with the picture, not the timeline: **location, product, isolation, resources requested, life safety**. Save chronology for the second beat.
Want to run a {practiceWord}? I can pick the one targeted to your weakest concept right now.

fallback.text: That one's outside the course library I'm grounded in, so I'll do my best — but treat my answer as a starting point, not the last word. **For anything urgent or high-stakes, check with a peer, supervisor, or the right professional first.** If you can give me a little more context, I'll try to point you to a chapter or {practiceWord} in your library that's adjacent to what you're asking. Or I can just take a swing at it and you can tell me if I'm warm.

escalation.text: That sounds urgent and outside what I should advise on. Please contact your supervisor or emergency services. I can resume coaching afterwards.
